h1: The 6 Best Wireless Printers for Printing From iPhone and iPad, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best iPhone & iPad Printers: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 wireless printers for iPhone and iPad compared on AirPrint support, ink system, document feeders and duplex printing.
summary: The Epson EcoTank ET-4800 is the best printer for iPhone and iPad households that print every week, with refillable ink tanks, an automatic document feeder and Ethernet. The EcoTank ET-2800 is the cheaper tank option, the Canon TS5320 states AirPrint support directly, and the HP DeskJet 4355 is the low-cost entry point if you remember to cancel the ink trial.
intro: The printer that is cheapest to buy is rarely the one that is cheapest to run, and iPhone owners find that out at the first ink warning. A phone has no driver disc and no USB cable, so what you are really buying is a wireless connection, an ink system and a companion app, and the ink system is where the money goes over three years.

This ranking is built around that idea. We reviewed six wireless all-in-ones from their spec sheets and listings, comparing ink design, document feeders, duplex printing, connectivity and the iOS app each one uses. We have not assumed any feature the listing does not state.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-4800 Wireless All-in-One Cartridge-Free Supertank Printer with ADF and Ethernet
products.verdict: Refillable tanks, an auto document feeder, Ethernet and fax in one reliable home-office machine.
products.description:
The ET-4800 is a cartridge-free supertank all-in-one with an auto document feeder, built-in fax, Ethernet plus Wi-Fi, and the Epson Smart Panel app for iOS. Ink comes from refillable tanks you top up from bottles rather than from replaceable cartridges.

It takes first place because it is the only model here that solves both recurring problems at once. The tank system removes the per-cartridge markup that makes cheap inkjets expensive over time, and the feeder lets you scan or copy a stack of pages from your phone without lifting the lid for each sheet. Ethernet is a quiet bonus: a wired connection avoids the dropped-Wi-Fi problems that frustrate phone printing. It outranks the ET-2800 because that unit lacks the feeder, fax and wired port.

Buy it if you run a home office, handle school paperwork or print several times a week. Skip it if you print only a few pages a month, since the price sits in the $100 to $200 bracket and a basic model would do.
cons: Costs more up front than cartridge models
products.idealFor: Home offices and families that print and scan weekly.
products.skipIf: You print a handful of pages a month.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-2800 Wireless Color All-in-One Cartridge-Free Ink Supertank Printer
products.verdict: The same refillable ink concept as the ET-4800, stripped down to the essentials.
products.description:
The ET-2800 is a wireless color all-in-one with refillable ink tanks, a flatbed scanner and the Epson Smart Panel app. Startup ink bottles are included, so the printer is ready to run without an extra purchase.

It ranks second because it delivers the ink economics that matter most to iPhone and iPad users, who tend to print photos, forms and homework in irregular bursts. Tank ink also sits in the machine for long gaps better than cartridges that dry up when unused. Against the ET-4800 you give up the document feeder, Ethernet and fax, so scanning a multi-page contract means lifting the lid sheet by sheet.

It is the best fit for a student household or a family that prints a few dozen pages a month. Skip it if you scan multi-page documents regularly.
pros: Refillable tanks keep ink costs low
Smart Panel app handles iOS printing
products.idealFor: Students and families who print in occasional bursts.
products.skipIf: You need to scan multi-page documents.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS5320 All in One Wireless Printer
products.verdict: AirPrint is named right on the listing, plus five separate ink tanks and a compact body.
products.description:
The TS5320 is a compact wireless all-in-one that lists AirPrint directly, uses five individual ink tanks and works with Alexa. It has a flatbed scanner with no document feeder, and it comes in black and a white finish.

It ranks third because AirPrint means your iPhone or iPad finds the printer on the network and prints from the share sheet with no app to install. Five separate tanks are also easier on the wallet than a single tri-color cartridge, since you only replace the color that has run out. The tradeoff is long-run ink cost: cartridges still cost far more per page than a tank printer, and the scanner has no feeder.

Choose it if you want the simplest iOS printing experience and print mostly photos or short documents. Skip it if you print heavily, because the Epson tank models are cheaper to run.
pros: Five separate ink tanks save waste
cons: Cartridge ink costs more over time
products.idealFor: Casual iOS users who want printing with no app setup.
products.skipIf: You print heavily and care about per-page cost.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TR4720 All-in-One Wireless Printer with Auto Document Feeder and Mobile Printing
products.verdict: The cheapest way to get an auto document feeder and fax in a compact printer.
products.description:
The TR4720 is a compact wireless all-in-one that scans through an automatic feeder, includes a fax modem, and prints from iOS via the Canon PRINT app. It sits in the $50 to $100 bracket.

It places fourth because the feeder is rare at this price, and it is the main reason to choose it. Scanning a ten-page document from your phone without opening the lid for each sheet is a real time saver for freelancers and small-business owners. Compared with the Canon TS5320 above, the TR4720 does not name AirPrint on its listing, so you should verify that your device sees it on the network, and the cartridge-based ink system makes it a better buy for light use than heavy.

It suits a home office that prints a little, scans a lot and still needs a fax line. Skip it if photo quality or low running cost is the priority.
pros: Auto document feeder at a low price
cons: Cartridge ink is costly per page
AirPrint not named on the listing
products.idealFor: Freelancers who scan more than they print.
products.skipIf: You print often or care about photo output.

products.name: Brother Work Smart 1360 Wireless Color Inkjet All-in-One Printer with Automatic Duplex Printing
products.verdict: Automatic two-sided printing and a color screen for people who print longer documents.
products.description:
The Work Smart 1360 is a wireless color inkjet all-in-one with automatic duplex printing, a 1.8 inch color display and a flatbed scanner. It ships with a Refresh Subscription ink trial.

It ranks fifth because duplex printing is the one feature that saves both paper and tedium on longer documents. Manually flipping pages is where most home printing goes wrong, with sheets reversed or jammed, and an automatic unit avoids that. The color display also makes it easier to check status without opening an app. The catch is the subscription: an ink trial can turn into a monthly charge if you forget it, and the flatbed has no feeder.

Buy it if you print essays, reports or recipes and want two-sided output without effort. Skip it if you would prefer to own your ink supply outright rather than rent it.
cons: Ink trial may become a subscription
products.idealFor: Students and remote workers who print long documents.

products.name: HP DeskJet 4355 Wireless All-in-One Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: A low-price iOS-friendly printer that depends on you managing the ink subscription.
products.description:
The DeskJet 4355 is a wireless color all-in-one with the HP Smart app for iOS, a flatbed scanner and a 3-month Instant Ink trial. The app also advertises AI-capable HP Smart features.

It lands last because the printer is cheap and the ink is not. The HP Smart app is a polished way to scan, print and share from an iPhone, and the entry cost is among the lowest in this group. The cost is that Instant Ink is a subscription, and cancelling after the trial is something you have to remember. Without it, cartridge costs rise quickly, and the machine has no feeder, no duplex and no tank system.

It works for a household that prints a few pages a month and wants a very low entry price. Skip it if you want predictable ink costs or you often print long documents.
pros: HP Smart app is polished on iOS
products.idealFor: Light users who want the lowest entry price.
products.skipIf: You print often or dislike ink subscriptions.

whatMatters.detail: AirPrint is Apple's built-in printing system, so a compatible printer appears in the iOS share sheet with no driver. Maker apps such as Epson Smart Panel, HP Smart and Canon PRINT add scanning and maintenance tools. Look for AirPrint named on the listing, and treat a vendor app alone as a fallback.

Cartridge printers are cheap to buy and expensive to feed, while tank printers cost more up front and far less per page. Subscription programs such as Instant Ink bill monthly, which can suit steady printing and punish occasional use. Check which system the printer uses before comparing prices.

A feeder pulls a stack of sheets through the scanner so you do not have to lift the lid for every page. It saves real time on contracts, taxes and school paperwork. Look for ADF in the specs, because flatbed-only machines handle single pages only.

Automatic duplex prints on both sides of a sheet without you flipping pages. It halves paper use for long documents and avoids the jams that come with manual flipping. The listing will say automatic duplex; manual duplex support is a weaker alternative.

Wi-Fi is enough for most homes, but Ethernet gives a stable wired fallback when the wireless signal drops. Wi-Fi printers that sleep deeply can also take a few seconds to wake. Check for Ethernet if your printer sits far from the router.

faq.q: Does an iPhone need a special app to print?
faq.a: Not if the printer supports AirPrint, because the iOS share sheet finds it automatically on your network. The maker apps from Epson, HP and Canon add scanning and maintenance, and they are a useful fallback if AirPrint does not detect the printer.

faq.q: What is the common mistake when buying a cheap printer?
faq.a: Judging by the purchase price and ignoring ink. Cartridge costs and subscriptions can exceed the printer's price within a year of regular use. Compare the ink system first, then the sticker.

faq.q: Is an EcoTank worth it over a cheaper inkjet?
faq.a: If you print weekly, yes. The tank design costs more at checkout but far less per page, and the ink survives idle weeks better than cartridges. If you print rarely, a cheap inkjet is fine.

faq.q: How do I set up a printer with an iPhone?
faq.a: Connect the printer to your Wi-Fi network using its control panel or maker app, then open the share sheet on your phone and tap Print. Your iPhone and printer must be on the same network for AirPrint to see it.

faq.q: How do I avoid being charged for an ink subscription?
faq.a: Set a calendar reminder for the end of the trial and cancel in the maker's app or account page before it ends. The HP DeskJet 4355 and Brother Work Smart 1360 both include trial offers, so check the terms at setup.

faq.q: Will a printer scan from my iPad too?
faq.a: Yes, through the maker's app or the iOS scanner tools, depending on the printer. A document feeder, found on the Epson ET-4800 and Canon TR4720, lets you scan multi-page documents from the iPad in one pass.

finalTake: The Epson EcoTank ET-4800 is the best choice for anyone who prints or scans on a regular basis, thanks to refillable ink, a feeder and Ethernet. The ET-2800 is the cheaper way to get the same ink savings, and the Canon TS5320 is the easiest pick for pure AirPrint convenience. Treat the HP DeskJet 4355 and the Brother 1360 as light-use machines, and cancel any ink trial before it renews.
